cards.#1: Jon Millman hand stamps, torches and paints copper in Melville, New York, and this is his replica of the marker that completed the career Grand Slam at the 2025 Masters. The finish comes off a torch rather than a plating line, so no two discs land in the same place tonally. Golf Life Metals sells it at $115.
cards.#2: The 2025 Players marker comes out of the same hands and the same copper as the Masters piece. Millman stamps, torches and paints every one in Melville, so a replica carries the same variation the original had. Golf Life Metals prices all of these at $115.
cards.#3: Tommy Fleetwood won the 2025 Tour Championship and Golf Life Metals sells the replica of the marker that went with him. The copper is stamped and torched by hand in a unit on Broadhollow Road, which is why the tone shifts from disc to disc. Millman charges $115.
cards.#4: Darren Clarke had one of these in his pocket for the 2021 Senior Open, which puts the shop’s tour record back further than the recent run suggests. The build is the same hand-stamped, torch-finished copper Golf Life Metals sells across the catalogue at $115.
cards.#5: Shane Lowry has a Ryder Cup piece in the Golf Life Metals catalogue, and the shop lists an official Ryder Cup marker alongside it. Both are hand-stamped copper at $115, torched and painted by hand in Melville rather than pressed and plated somewhere else.
cards.#6: Golf Life Metals has made markers for Jack Nicklaus, and the shop’s own line is “we’ve made for Jack, Tiger, Scottie.” The Nicklaus design sells to anybody at $115, in the same torched copper Millman uses for the tour work.
cards.#7: The Grand Slam design is the one Golf Life Metals sells to anybody, with no name attached to it. Millman stamps it into copper and finishes it with a torch the same way he does the tour replicas, at the same $115.
cards.#8: Shinnecock gets the full treatment, torched copper with hand-painted numerals, which is where the shop’s technique shows most clearly. Paint sitting down in a stamped recess reads at arm’s length in a way an etched disc never does. Golf Life Metals charges $115.
cards.#9: Golf Life Metals sells this one out of the same catalogue as the Nicklaus marker, six inches down the same page. The build does not change either: hand-stamped copper, torch finish, $115. The shop draws no distinction between the two in price or in method.
cards.#10: The blanks are raw copper discs at six dollars, sold for anybody who would rather do the stamping themselves. Nothing is torched and nothing is painted, which is the point of buying the metal before Millman gets to it. Six dollars is the floor of the catalogue.
cards.#11: Golf Life Metals has “Rory’s Masters markers (both)” at the top of its homepage, meaning the 2025 piece and this one from 2026. The shop also hosts a video called Making Rory’s Grand Slam Marker if you want to watch the copper go under the torch. It sells for the same $115 as the rest.
cards.#12: Seamus forges in Portland, striking every piece by hand so no two come out identical. This one is an anvil, struck on an anvil, in steel. At $36 it is about as literal as a maker’s mark gets.
cards.#13: The Sakura is a cherry blossom forged into copper and the prettiest shape Seamus hammers out. Copper takes a patina faster than steel does, so the petals will darken down into the recesses over a season of being handled. Seamus prices it at $48.
cards.#14: The horseshoe is steel and sits in the $48 tier, which is where the more involved shapes live. Seamus forges each one by hand in Portland, so the curve and the nail holes land slightly differently every time.
cards.#15: The Labyrinth is a maze stamped into copper, and from a foot away it stops reading as a maze and starts reading as texture. That is a useful quality in an object that spends most of its life face down on a green. Seamus sells it at $36.
cards.#16: The dimple pattern is forged into steel so the marker carries the same surface as the ball it stands in for. Seamus plays that straight, with nothing printed on it and nothing explaining it. The price is $36.
cards.#17: Touch Gorse is named for the stuff you will be visiting later in the round, forged in bronze at $36. Bronze is the warmest of the three metals Seamus works in and the one that sits between the copper and the steel.
cards.#18: Fyfe forges in Scotland and puts its house mark into bronze at £25. Hand striking means the edges and the depth of the stamp shift from one disc to the next, which is the argument for a forged marker over a printed one.
cards.#19: The copper version costs the same £25 and takes a patina faster than the bronze does. It carries the same Fyfe house mark, forged by hand in Scotland, so the stamp lands at a slightly different depth on every disc that comes off the anvil.
cards.#20: The Brave is Fyfe’s other design, in copper at £25, hand forged in Scotland like the rest of the shop’s work. Copper is the metal that changes most in a pocket, so this is the one that will look least like it did on arrival.
cards.#21: Old Tom Morris goes into copper at Hame, in a £25 run that has now sold out. The shop works in small batches, so a sold-out marker there sits closer to a finished edition than to a restock problem.
cards.#22: Matchstick Golf has Chunk from The Goonies doing the truffle shuffle in enamel, on a golf course, for twenty dollars. The same catalogue holds a dinosaur caddie and three flavours of a Gatorade parody, and this is still the one that stops people. Nobody asked for it, and it remains the best thing the shop makes.
cards.#23: The VW bus is an orange split-screen in enamel at twenty dollars. Matchstick keeps its whole catalogue at that price, which is why the references can be this specific without anybody having to think hard about buying one.
cards.#24: Teddy Roosevelt gets the enamel treatment, pince-nez and all, at twenty dollars. Matchstick draws its markers as small illustrations rather than logos, so a face still reads once it has been shrunk to the size of a coin.
cards.#25: The Chef Skull is a skull in a toque over crossed bones, in enamel at twenty dollars. Matchstick runs a catalogue where that sits next to a president and a dinosaur and none of it needs explaining.
cards.#26: The Caddysaurus is a dinosaur carrying a bag, which is the entire idea and enough of one. Matchstick prices it at twenty dollars like everything else in the enamel line, and the drawing survives being shrunk to the size of a coin.
cards.#27: The pirate flag reads THE COAST across a Jolly Roger, in enamel at twenty dollars. Matchstick keeps the drawing simple enough that it still holds together at coin size. Twenty dollars is the flat price across the enamel line, whatever the reference.
cards.#28: The Josh Allen marker is a Bills tribute drawn to look licensed without ever claiming to be, at twenty dollars. Matchstick draws these as illustrations rather than logos, which is how it gets within touching distance of a team mark. Buffalo will buy every one the shop makes.
cards.#29: Seamus forged The Dude into bronze at $36, which is a Big Lebowski reference rendered in metal instead of print. Hand striking gives the face a slightly different depth on every disc, and the bronze will dull down over a season.
cards.#30: Seamus put the 1986 Nicklaus call into bronze, “Yes Sir!” stamped into a $36 disc. Forging it rather than printing it means the words sit below the surface and will still be legible long after the finish has gone dark.
cards.#31: MARK & LONA is a Japanese label and its skull marker is iron rather than the copper or bronze most of the category works in. At ¥10,125 it costs more than any marker outside the hand-forged copper tier, which is a lot of money for something you leave on a green.
cards.#32: Pins & Aces holds a real Coca-Cola licence, which is not what you expect from a golf accessory brand charging $14.95. The contour bottle is rendered correctly, curves and all, rather than approximated into a generic soda shape.
cards.#33: The polar bear comes off the same Coca-Cola licence at the same $14.95. Pins & Aces has to treat the artwork the way a licensee does, so the bear is the bear rather than a lookalike drawn to stay out of trouble.
cards.#34: Blazy Susan makes pink rolling papers and Pins & Aces has a licence with them, which produced a co-branded golf ball marker at $14.95. The silhouette is the more restrained of the two designs, which is a relative statement.
cards.#35: The Smoke Pink version puts the colour front and centre at $14.95, on the same Blazy Susan licence. Pins & Aces runs two real trademark deals at once, which is two more than most of the category has managed.
cards.#36: SWAG Golf has a Tito’s licence and prices the marker at $66.66, the house number the brand puts on nearly everything. Splash Of Grape is the louder of the two Tito’s designs and makes no attempt to hide what it is advertising.
cards.#37: The Water Hazard version runs the same $66.66 and the same Tito’s licence, with the joke moved from the glass to the pond. SWAG does not discount for a second colourway. Both designs come off a real trademark deal, which is uncommon at any price in the category.
cards.#38: Riviera has the 2026 U.S. Women’s Open and Seamus forged the marker for it rather than printing one. The stamp goes into the metal, so it will still be there once the finish has worn off the high points. Seamus sells it at $36.
cards.#39: The 2025 Ryder Cup marker is bronze at $48, sitting in the tier where Seamus puts the more involved work. A forged commemorative ages differently to a printed one, which is most of the reason to pay this for a disc.
cards.#40: Golf by QD is a Mexican brand that mostly makes caddie crowns, and the Ocean Course marker is the outlier in its catalogue. Kiawah lands at $19, which is a low price for a course that most brands would charge a premium to put on anything.
cards.#41: Sounder comes from Cleeve Hill in Gloucestershire and named a marker after the course rather than after a tournament. At £5 it cost less than a pint, and the run sold out. The brand does the same thing with its bag towel.
cards.#42: The combo tin packages the same Cleeve Hill idea at £65, which is a different proposition to a single £5 disc. Sixty-five pounds buys a set in a tin rather than a marker in a bag, so it lands as a gift more than a purchase. Sounder sold through that one as well.
cards.#43: Azalea is a hole name that does not need explaining to anybody who watches golf in April. Pins & Aces made a marker out of it at $14.95 and the run sold out. Everything the brand makes sits at that price, tournament references included.
cards.#44: 5280 is Denver’s elevation in feet and the shorthand the city uses for itself, which makes it a marker for people who play at altitude and like to mention it. Pins & Aces sells it at $14.95.
cards.#45: The Liberty Bell marker is Philadelphia in enamel, crack included, at $14.95. Pins & Aces keeps its city markers to one obvious landmark each and leaves the rest alone. Every one of them costs the same $14.95, whatever the city.
cards.#46: Matchstick made three flavours of a Gatorade bottle relabelled as Putterade, of which lemon-lime is the one everybody pictures first. The shape sits close enough to the original that you read the bottle before you read the joke. Twenty dollars, in enamel, like the rest of the line.
cards.#47: The iced coffee comes with a straw in it and a gold version alongside the standard one. Matchstick keeps both at twenty dollars, which is the price of every enamel marker the shop makes. The gold is the same drawing in a different finish.
cards.#48: The Old Fashioned is a rocks glass with an orange peel and a cherry, drawn small enough to sit under a ball. Matchstick renders the drink rather than a brand, so nothing about it needs a licence, and the price stays at twenty dollars.
cards.#49: The Transfusion is the drink every muni sells and nobody outside golf has heard of, which makes it the most inside reference Matchstick has put on a disc. It sells for twenty dollars like everything else in the enamel line.
cards.#50: The flaming coffee mug has a face on it and is on fire, which is a fair account of a seven-thirty tee time. Matchstick draws it in the same enamel as the rest of the drinks line and prices it at twenty dollars.
cards.#51: Fella Golf is a European brand selling in euros, and its pizza slice splits into two markers so a pair can share one purchase. The double format is unusual in a category that almost always sells singles. Fifteen euros.
cards.#52: The red Solo cup gets rendered in miniature at $14.95, which is a specific kind of American object to put on a green. Pins & Aces sells it next to the ice cubes and the two are made to be used together.
cards.#53: The ice cubes are two cubes in enamel at $14.95, made to sit alongside the red cup. Pins & Aces builds most of its drinks line in pairs like this rather than as one-offs.
cards.#54: SWAG Golf put a red, white and blue rocket pop on a marker and charged $66.66 for it, the same number the brand puts on nearly everything. The colours read from a distance, which is more than most markers manage.
cards.#55: Seamus and Pendleton have a longer relationship than a marker suggests, since Pendleton supplies the wool for the Seamus towels. The sugar skulls come in an oil can finish, the darkest thing in the Seamus line and the one that hides the forging marks least. Seamus charges $36.
cards.#56: Quiet Golf sends the design and Seamus swings the hammer, which is how all three markers in the partnership were made. The pennant is steel at $35 and the run sold out. A collaboration piece gets the same Portland hand work as the house line.
cards.#57: Parmore worked with the designer Posterlad on this one and came away with the cleanest graphic of any collaboration marker in the category. Ten pounds is a low price for a piece of actual design work rather than a logo scaled to fit.
cards.#58: Random Golf Club and Northwood put both names on one disc and priced it at ten dollars. The run sold out. Ten dollars puts it at the bottom of the collaboration tier, where most of the other two-name markers sit closer to thirty-five.
cards.#59: Malbon made this one for Shanghai Buckets, which marks a store rather than a tournament and tells you where the brand’s attention sits. Thirty-eight dollars puts it above the enamel tier and below the forged copper.
cards.#60: The Nimbus version runs the same series at the same $38, another Malbon location getting a disc of its own. Buckets is the brand’s store programme, so these work as souvenirs of having been somewhere rather than of having played something.
cards.#61: Seamus forged an artist edition for Press Golf and the subject is a panda tiger, which is exactly as odd as it sounds. The forging is the same Portland hand work as the house line, at $36.
cards.#62: The owl is bronze at $35, with Quiet Golf sending the design and Seamus doing the forging. It sold out, which is what happened to all three markers in that partnership, each of them priced the same and each in a different metal.
cards.#63: The monogram is copper at $35, the third piece from the same partnership and the plainest of them. Copper is the metal that moves most, so a monogram stamped into it will look older than it is inside a season. It sold out with the others.
cards.#64: Winston Collection makes its markers in leather instead of metal, and the Tradition is the tidier of the two finishes. Eighteen dollars buys something that will crease rather than patina, which is a different way for an object to record having been used.
cards.#65: Walker Golf sells the crest in three finishes at once, black, green and brushed gold, for A$39.95 out of Australia. Three at a time is a different proposition to the single-disc impulse buy the rest of the category runs on.
cards.#66: Birds of Condor built the At The Turn set around a hot dog, a beer and a pie in enamel. The set costs A$39.95 and is an accurate account of what actually gets bought at an Australian turn.
cards.#67: The Blockbusters set puts three film references into one A$39.95 pack, in the same format as the At The Turn markers. Birds of Condor sells its enamel in sets rather than singles, which is a rarer approach than it sounds.
cards.#68: The pull-up leather version costs the same $18 and ages the way a wallet does, lightening where it bends and darkening where it gets handled. Almost nobody else in the category works in leather at all.
cards.#69: The flame pin costs six dollars and clips magnetically to a hat rather than sitting on a green. Matchstick uses the same drawing style it puts on the markers, shrunk down further. Six dollars matches a raw copper blank, which is the other thing at the bottom of the range.
cards.#70: Ten dollars gets you whatever Matchstick decides to send, and the product photo is a question mark. Everything the shop makes in enamel sells at twenty, so the draw is a discount on the format as much as a gamble. It is a sensible way to move odd stock.
cards.#71: Left of Field works out of Sydney and prices in Australian dollars, so A$10 is about as low as a designed marker goes. The flower comes in silver and sage, quieter than most things at that price.
cards.#72: The script marker sold out at A$7 in dark green, with the lettering doing all the work. Left of Field works out of Sydney and prices in Australian dollars, and it keeps the markers cheap enough that losing one in the rough costs nothing.
cards.#73: Eastside Golf sells a magnetic coin marker at $13 and this run has gone. The magnetic format means it lives on a hat clip rather than loose in a pocket with the tees, and thirteen dollars puts it under most of the enamel tier.
cards.#74: Vessel makes bags first and the marker follows the same logic, plain metal at $15 and made to disappear into a pocket of one. Nothing on it announces anything. Fifteen dollars is the going rate for a marker with no drawing on it.
cards.#75: Casualist put an eight-point star with an eye at the centre on a £15 marker and sold through the run. The graphic sits closer to a tattoo flash sheet than to anything else in the category.
cards.#76: Radmor calls this one the BobRad and prices it at $15. Fifteen dollars is the tier where most brands stop trying, and a plain disc at that price still does the only job a marker has.
cards.#77: GOLF GEEK sits inside a comic-book speech bubble on this one, in enamel at A$19.95. Birds of Condor is Australian and prices in Australian dollars, so the conversion works in your favour. The brand mostly sells its enamel in sets, and this is one of the singles.
